strengths: Novel and theoretically grounded combination of the Adjoint Matching stochastic-control framework with weak-form PDE residuals to fine-tune flow-matching models, extended to jointly evolve a latent parameter field alongside the state — this addresses the practically important setting where paired parameter-state training data is unavailable.

The use of weak-form (rather than strong-form) residuals via randomly sampled compactly-supported Wendland test functions is a sensible and numerically stable design choice, well justified via integration-by-parts derivations for both PDE systems studied.

Broad set of experimental settings (denoising of noisy observations, sparse-observation guidance, 3D super-resolution with boundary constraints, and misspecified boundary conditions) demonstrates the flexibility of the framework.

The proposed running-cost regularizer (λf) that anchors the fine-tuned parameter trajectory to the base-model's inferred parameter is a useful practical mechanism to prevent mode collapse/diversity loss during fine-tuning, and its effect is clearly illustrated (Fig. 2, Table 2).
Reasonably detailed appendices (datasets, architecture, training algorithm, hyperparameters) support reproducibility, and the authors state code/data release.
weaknesses: Experimental validation is narrow: only two canonical, synthetic PDE systems (Darcy flow and a linear acoustic wave equation) at modest resolution, with no real observational data or more complex/coupled/nonlinear PDEs, despite the paper's stated motivation of scientific inverse problems in atmospheric/seismic/medical domains.

Quantitative comparison to prior physics-constrained generative baselines is very limited — despite an extensive related-work section citing PBFM (Baldan et al. 2025), Bastek et al. (2024), DiffusionPDE (Huang et al. 2024), PhyDA, Utkarsh et al. (2025), etc., the only empirical baseline comparison is a single qualitative comparison to ECI (Cheng et al. 2024) in the appendix, with no quantitative metrics reported for it.

Evaluation relies heavily on qualitative visual figures and small sample counts (128–256 samples) for quantitative tables; no confidence intervals/repeated seeds are reported for the main comparisons, and no standard generative-quality metrics (e.g., FID or similar) are used alongside the custom pointwise statistics.

The method has many interacting hyperparameters (λx, λα, λf, test-function scale ranges, tail-refinement schedule, loss clipping thresholds) and the paper shows the method is fairly sensitive to these choices (e.g., mode collapse without regularization, need for careful λx tuning in the misspecification experiment), raising concerns about robustness and ease of practical use.

The authors explicitly characterize the experiments as "preliminary" in the conclusion, and no ablation is provided to justify the necessity of the more complex joint vector-field evolution of α over the simpler push-forward-through-φ baseline mentioned in the method section.

Scalability is a concern: the 3D super-resolution experiment requires ~12 hours of fine-tuning on a single GPU for a relatively small case, and no discussion of scaling behavior to larger/more realistic 3D or multi-physics systems is provided.

The comparison with ECI is acknowledged by the authors themselves to be somewhat unfair (gradient-free vs. gradient-based, no PDE awareness), weakening the strength of this sole empirical baseline comparison.

strengths: Novel and technically interesting combination of Adjoint Matching (a recent stochastic-optimal-control-based fine-tuning framework for flow models) with weak-form PDE residuals to achieve numerically stable physics-constrained fine-tuning.

Addresses a genuinely important and underexplored problem: enforcing parameter-dependent PDE constraints and jointly inferring latent physical parameters without access to paired state-parameter training data.

The joint evolution scheme for state x and latent parameter alpha, including the surrogate base flow via the inverse predictor and the regularization term tying fine-tuned parameter trajectories to base-model estimates, is a thoughtful architectural contribution.

Covers a reasonably broad set of task types (denoising, sparse-observation guidance, super-resolution with reflective boundaries, misspecified boundary conditions), showing some versatility of the framework.
Detailed appendices with implementation specifics, hyperparameters, and some reproducibility-oriented descriptions (e.g., test-function design, training algorithm pseudocode).
weaknesses: Evaluation is limited to only two canonical, relatively simple linear PDE systems (Darcy flow and linear acoustic wave equation) with binary-valued coefficient fields (a in {3,12}, c in {2,3}), which is a significant simplification that may not stress-test the method's ability to handle realistic continuous or more complex latent parameters.

Despite an extensive related-work section citing many closely related physics-constrained generative/diffusion methods (Bastek et al. 2024, PBFM, PhyDA, DiffusionPDE, Utkarsh et al., Zhang & Zou), the paper provides essentially no quantitative comparison against any of them; the only baseline comparison (ECI) is relegated to the appendix and explicitly described by the authors as 'not entirely fair.'

Quantitative evidence is thin: small sample counts for evaluation (e.g., 20, 128, 256 samples), a single residual table per experiment, and heavy reliance on qualitative/visual figures to support central claims (e.g., 'as λx increases, samples conform progressively better').

No systematic study or principled method for selecting the key hyperparameters λx and λf, which the results show have a large and somewhat unpredictable effect on fidelity vs. diversity trade-offs; the authors acknowledge this as an unresolved issue for future work.
The paper itself characterizes its experiments as 'preliminary' in the conclusion, undermining confidence in the robustness and generality of the claimed results.

No real-world or higher-complexity (e.g., nonlinear, multi-physics, chaotic) PDE systems are tested, despite such settings being highlighted in the introduction as key motivating applications (seismic inversion, atmospheric modeling, medical imaging).

Lack of computational cost analysis/comparison (training and inference overhead) relative to baseline fine-tuning or inference-time projection approaches, despite Adjoint Matching and weak-residual evaluation being nontrivially expensive.

Error bars/statistical rigor are inconsistent across tables, and some conclusions (e.g., 'diversity preserved with regularization') rely on a narrow set of metrics that may not fully capture distributional fidelity.

strengths: Novel and technically well-motivated combination of Adjoint Matching-based stochastic control fine-tuning with weak-form PDE residuals, addressing a real gap: enforcing parameter-dependent physical constraints without access to paired parameter-solution training data.

The joint evolution scheme for simultaneously generating states and latent parameters (via a surrogate base flow derived from an inverse predictor, plus a regularization term anchoring fine-tuned parameters to base estimates) is a creative architectural contribution that plausibly balances constraint satisfaction with preservation of sample diversity.

Broad and relevant experimental coverage: denoising of noisy observational data, guidance from sparse parameter observations, 3D super-resolution with boundary enforcement, and robustness to model misspecification, demonstrating the versatility of the framework across multiple inverse-problem settings.

Extensive implementation details and ablations are provided in the appendix (architecture modifications, test-function design, training heuristics, hyperparameters per experiment), which aids reproducibility and transparency.

Thoughtful discussion of trade-offs via the regularization hyperparameter λf, with clear qualitative and quantitative (Table 2) evidence that naively increasing fine-tuning strength without regularization causes mode collapse/loss of diversity, while the proposed regularization avoids this.

Includes a direct comparison against a relevant inference-time baseline (ECI) on the boundary misspecification task, providing some empirical grounding for claimed advantages over projection-based approaches.
weaknesses: The core theoretical machinery (Adjoint Matching) is adopted wholesale from Domingo-Enrich et al. 2025; the main novelty lies in the joint state-parameter augmentation and weak-residual reward design, which is somewhat incremental relative to the cited related work (e.g., PBFM, DiffusionPDE, Physics-Constrained Flow Matching), several of which are not empirically compared against despite being closely related.

Evaluation is restricted to two relatively simple, low-dimensional, synthetic canonical PDE systems (2D Darcy flow with binary permeability, 2D/3D linear acoustic wave equation); no real-world data, more complex/nonlinear/multi-physics systems, or higher-resolution 3D problems are considered, limiting evidence of generality and practical significance.

Quantitative evaluation relies on small sample counts in several experiments (e.g., 20 samples for the acoustic/3D super-resolution task, 128–256 for Darcy), and lacks statistical significance testing or broader baseline comparisons (e.g., against PINN-based inversion, other physics-informed diffusion/flow approaches) beyond the single ECI comparison restricted to one experiment.

There is no direct validation of recovered latent parameters against ground-truth parameter fields (beyond residual-based proxies and qualitative visualization); since the inverse predictor is trained only to minimize weak residual rather than supervised against true α, the identifiability and correctness of recovered parameters (versus merely residual-consistent but potentially non-physical α) is not rigorously examined.

The authors themselves characterize the experiments as "preliminary," and several hyperparameters (λx, λf, test-function length-scales) require manual tuning per task/dataset with no principled or adaptive selection strategy, raising concerns about practical applicability and robustness outside the tested settings.

No computational cost/runtime comparison against baseline methods (e.g., ECI, PBFM, or standard PINN-based inversion) is provided, despite Adjoint Matching fine-tuning being noted elsewhere as potentially expensive; the appendix reports runtimes (e.g., ~12h for the 3D task) without context relative to alternatives.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and underexplored gap: enforcing parameter-dependent PDE constraints in generative models without requiring paired solution-parameter training data, which is important for realistic scientific inverse problems.

Solid theoretical extension of the Adjoint Matching framework (Domingo-Enrich et al., 2025), including a well-justified scaled memoryless noise schedule (Lemma 1) that provides a practical stabilization/exploration knob.

The joint evolution of state and latent parameter via a surrogate base flow derived from an inverse predictor is a clean and reasonably novel architectural idea that enables amortized parameter inference during fine-tuning.

Extensive empirical evaluation across four distinct PDE families (Darcy, elasticity, Helmholtz, Stokes) plus a natural-image application, with sensible baselines (vanilla FM, PBFM, ECI, ablations Base AM/Base AM+φ) and multiple complementary metrics (weak/strong residuals, MMD_x, MMD_α, SSIM diversity).

Careful and honest experimental design: deliberately introduces model misspecification (BC changes, damping mismatch, missing forcing) to test robustness, which is a meaningful and more realistic stress test than typical in-distribution physics-constrained generation papers.

Strong reproducibility effort: detailed appendices with full architecture specs, hyperparameters, weak-residual derivations (with integration-by-parts) for each PDE, and full training algorithm (Algorithm 1).
Ablations (Fig. 3, 5, 9-11, 13) clearly illustrate controllable trade-offs between residual reduction, distributional fidelity, and sample diversity, giving practitioners actionable guidance.
Cross-domain demonstration on natural images (parametric recoloring + PickScore) shows the framework generalizes beyond PDE settings, strengthening the generality claim.
weaknesses: The method has many interacting components (weak residuals, joint flow, regularization term f(α), scaled noise schedule, correction heads) making it difficult to cleanly attribute gains to individual design choices; while ablations exist, the overall system is complex and could be hard to reproduce/tune in practice.

All PDE experiments use small, synthetic, low-resolution (64x64) 2D benchmarks with simple two-phase or Gaussian-random-field coefficient structures; it remains unclear how the method scales to higher-dimensional, more realistic, or real observational scientific data.

Several quantitative results show large error bars/overlapping confidence intervals across methods and hyperparameters (e.g., Table 2, Table 13), raising questions about the statistical robustness of some comparative claims (e.g., Helmholtz AM vs Base AM improvements are often within one standard deviation).

For the Stokes experiment, weak/strong residuals are comparable across ablations and the main advantage of the joint model is confined to MMD_α, a relatively narrow win that is not strongly emphasized as a limitation in the main text.

The PBFM baseline is arguably placed at an structural disadvantage since it is a training-time method evaluated under deliberately introduced misspecification; while the authors acknowledge this, it complicates fair comparison and interpretation of the reported gains over PBFM.

Core theoretical contribution (adjoint matching for reward tilting) is inherited from prior work; the paper's main novelty—joint state-parameter evolution via a surrogate base flow and residual correction heads—is somewhat incremental from an architectural standpoint (essentially conditioning/augmenting existing backbones).

No real-world (non-synthetic) scientific dataset or downstream task (e.g., actual sensor data, benchmark inverse problems used in the PINN/data-assimilation literature) is used to validate practical utility, limiting evidence for real-world impact.

The natural-image experiment, while interesting, is a fairly different problem (parametric recoloring is not a genuine physical/PDE constraint) and its connection to the main physics-constrained narrative feels somewhat tangential and under-analyzed quantitatively (only qualitative images shown, no numeric reward/diversity trade-off table).

strengths: Addresses a genuinely under-explored problem: enforcing parameter-dependent PDE constraints in generative flow models without requiring paired solution-parameter training data.
Technically grounded extension of the Adjoint Matching framework, including a (modest) theoretical contribution in the form of a scaled memoryless noise schedule with a formal proof of consistency.

Reasonably broad empirical coverage across four PDE families (Darcy, elasticity, Helmholtz, Stokes) plus a natural-image cross-domain demonstration, with extensive appendix detail on datasets, architectures, and residual derivations (weak forms, test functions) that aids reproducibility.

Includes several relevant baselines/ablations (PBFM, ECI, Base AM, Base AM+phi) and reports both PDE residuals and distributional (MMD) metrics, attempting a multi-faceted evaluation rather than a single metric.

The joint state-parameter flow idea and the regularization mechanism (f(alpha) penalty) are a sensible, clearly motivated design for balancing physics-consistency against distributional/sample fidelity.
weaknesses: The method introduces a large number of interacting hyperparameters (lambda_x, lambda_alpha, lambda_f, kappa, K, K_last, time-tilting q, LCT thresholds) that appear to require per-dataset, per-task manual tuning; the extensive sweep tables in the appendix read more as a hyperparameter search than evidence of a robust, generally applicable method, and no principled/automatic selection strategy is proposed.

Comparisons to PBFM are acknowledged by the authors themselves to be unfair, since PBFM is a training-time method evaluated under a setting that deliberately introduces train/fine-tune model misspecification, placing it 'at a disadvantage' by the authors' own admission -- this undermines the validity of the main quantitative comparisons used to argue superiority.

PBFM is also trained with a much smaller batch size than the base FM/AM models due to memory constraints (16 vs 128), confounding the comparison further and making it unclear whether reported gaps reflect the proposed method's merits or baseline undertraining.

The architecture used for the proposed method is augmented with substantial additional capacity (correction U-Net heads, ~6M-9M extra parameters) relative to baselines operating on the frozen base backbone; the performance gains could partly be attributable to this capacity increase rather than the core methodological contributions (weak residuals + joint flow + adjoint matching).

All PDE experiments are conducted on small-scale, synthetic 64x64 grid problems with simplified geometries and known closed-form governing equations; there is no evaluation on real observational data, higher resolution, 3D, time-dependent, or genuinely complex/noisy scientific datasets, limiting evidence of real-world significance.

The natural-image 'cross-domain utility' experiment (parametric recoloring to maximize PickScore) is not a physical constraint at all -- it is a stylistic/appearance optimization unrelated to PDE residuals, making the claimed bridging of 'generative modelling and physics-informed learning' to natural images somewhat superficial and tangential to the paper's stated contributions.

Many quantitative improvements over strong AM ablations (Base AM, Base AM+phi) are modest and often within overlapping error bars (e.g., Helmholtz Rweak 4.3 vs 4.9-5.6, Stokes Rweak comparable across AM variants), while the clearest gains (e.g., MMD_alpha in Stokes) are presented without strong statistical support beyond averaged error bars over a single seed set.

The core technical novelty is incremental: it largely combines existing components (Adjoint Matching from Domingo-Enrich et al., weak-form PDE residuals common in physics-informed learning, standard inverse-predictor networks) with one genuinely new but minor theoretical twist (noise schedule scaling); the conceptual contribution over prior inference-time/training-time physics-constrained generative methods is relatively narrow.

Qualitative figures (e.g., Fig. 2, 4, 6) are used to support central claims about denoising/regularization trade-offs without any accompanying quantitative per-sample statistics, making it hard to assess whether the depicted single examples are representative.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and underexplored problem: enforcing parameter-dependent PDE constraints on pretrained flow-matching models without requiring paired state-parameter training data, which is practically relevant in many scientific domains.

Technically grounded approach built on the Adjoint Matching framework, with an explicit construction of a joint state-parameter flow via a surrogate base flow induced by an inverse predictor, which is a reasonable and fairly novel extension.

Provides a theoretical contribution (Lemma 1) justifying a scaled memoryless noise schedule, extending the family of valid schedules beyond the canonical one from Domingo-Enrich et al., with practical benefits for numerical stability.

Extensive empirical evaluation across four distinct PDE families (Darcy, elasticity, Helmholtz, Stokes) covering different types of model misspecification (observation noise, boundary condition mismatch, damping mismatch, forcing mismatch), plus a creative cross-domain application to natural images.

Thorough ablation studies illustrating controllable trade-offs between residual reduction, distributional fidelity (MMD), and sample diversity (SSIM), which help contextualize the practical utility of the hyperparameters introduced.
Reasonably strong set of baselines/ablations (Base AM, Base AM+φ, PBFM, FM+ECI) that isolate the contribution of the joint parameter-state flow versus simpler alternatives.
Detailed appendix with dataset generation protocols, architecture specifications, and derivations of weak-form residuals for each PDE, supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: The method introduces a large number of interacting hyperparameters (λx, λα, λf, κ, test-function parameters, clipping thresholds), and the paper does not provide clear practical guidance on how a practitioner without access to a reference dataset would select these values, which limits real-world applicability.

All experiments are conducted on relatively small, synthetic 2D problems (64x64 grids) with simple geometries; there is no demonstration on more realistic, higher-resolution, or 3D/ time-dependent systems, leaving scalability of the adjoint-matching ODE solve and weak-residual computation largely untested.

No validation on real experimental/observational data; all PDE datasets are synthetically generated with hand-crafted misspecifications, which may not reflect the complexity of real inverse problems in practice.

The identifiability and correctness of the recovered latent parameters α is not rigorously analyzed — φ is trained only to minimize PDE residual, not to match ground-truth parameters, so it's unclear how faithfully recovered α correspond to true physical quantities beyond residual consistency.

The natural-image experiment, while an interesting cross-domain illustration, uses a color-transform as a stand-in for 'physics,' which is a fairly loose analogy and does not strongly substantiate the claimed broader applicability of the physics-constrained framework.

Comparisons to PBFM are somewhat confounded by the fact that PBFM is a training-time method evaluated under deliberately introduced misspecification that favors post-training approaches; this is acknowledged by the authors but still complicates fair comparison.

The paper's method, while combining existing techniques (Adjoint Matching, weak-form residuals, ConFIG-style baselines) in a new way, is somewhat incremental relative to the cited prior works (Domingo-Enrich et al. 2025, Baldan et al. 2025), and the core novelty is concentrated in the joint parameter-flow construction and noise-schedule scaling rather than a fundamentally new paradigm.
Uncertainty quantification, which is mentioned as a motivating application in the introduction and conclusion, is not actually evaluated or demonstrated in the experiments.
